rv.q: After watching Tracie Bennett’s electrifying interpretation of Garland in the intense production that opened on Monday night at the Belasco Theater, you feel exhilarated and exhausted, equally ready to dance down the street and crawl under a rock.
Bennett's performance is nothing short of extraordinary, a breathtaking impersonation that captures both Garland's incandescent talent and her tragic fragility.
It's hard to watch, but even harder not to watch.
Bennett doesn't just look and sound like Garland; she becomes her, capturing the desperate vulnerability and manic energy.
It’s a decent vehicle for a drunk driver.
Although the play offers a raw and shocking portrait of Garland, it quickly runs out of steam.
Beyond that, it's a sad spectacle that should (but doesn't) muster some resonance in light of such recent casualties of fame and addiction as Michael Jackson, Amy Winehouse and Whitney Houston.
That Bennett performs this show eight times a week is a marvel indeed; seeing it just once kind of wore me out.
Tracie Bennett's performance as Judy Garland is nothing short of extraordinary, capturing both the vulnerability and the fierce determination that defined the legend's final years.
When you have someone like Bennett carrying all the really important luggage, though, the trip will be worthwhile.
There are productions that exist solely to feature a spectacular star. This is one of them. Rush to the Belasco to catch Bennett and revel in her—and Garland’s—glory.
It's definitely the most energetic performance of the year.

Tribute and trash collide uneasily in 'End of the Rainbow,' a jacked-up portrait of Judy Garland that captures the legend at the end of her rope near the end of her life. It is not a pretty picture. Or an illuminating one.
A saving grace for this unsalvageable travesty is the superb five-piece ensemble that augments the piano during the concert sections.

The play, an attempt to document the conflicts that consumed one of America’s greatest artists, feels contrived and paints Judy in the worst possible light, as a shrewd manipulative drug addict losing control, frightened, and profoundly needy.
It's trash. Pulp rubbish by playwright Peter Quilter.
